newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission to adopt plan to fight transit fraud.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission to adopt plan to fight transit fraud.

text.p: The European Commission will propose a plan on Wednesday to fight illegal imports of cigarettes and alcohol which some say cost national and European Union coffers billions of dollars in lost taxes and duties.

The plan follows increasing evidence that huge quantities of cigarettes and alcohol are finding their way into the 15-nation, border-free market illegally because controls on transit freight, which is only supposed to cross the bloc's territory, are not tight enough.
The European Parliament estimated in March that as much as 30 billion European currency units ($33.9 billion) a year were being lost to transit fraud due to an obsolete paper-based control system.
But national governments have uncovered fraud cases amounting only to 1.27 billion Ecus in the period 1990-1996, a Commission official said on Tuesday.
The main solution was to introduce a computerised system enabling national customs authorities to trace goods until they effectively leave the Union, an EU source said, quoting the action plan.

The plan also suggests better coordination between customs administrations in the EU and their counterparts in the European Free Trade Association's four states -- Switzerland, Norway, Liechstenstein and Iceland -- and in central and eastern Europe.
Switzerland, which sits at the crossroads of Europe but is not an EU member, was identified in the parliament report as being one of the main hubs in the transit fraud business.
Among the other Commission proposals is a call for more frequent sealing of transit lorries and their identification with a 'T' symbol.

Under European transit rules, freight can cross the Union's territory and several neighbouring states tax free, with customs duties, value-added tax and excise duties payable only at the good's final, third-country destinations.
Cigarettes and alcohol are particularly prone to fraud because of the high duties levied in the Union, which in the case of cigarettes account for about three-quarters of the retail price.
